query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The dominant mechanism governing wear resistance and microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding in FeNiCrCoCu coatings is the formation of a stable, adherent oxide scale that acts as a barrier against direct metal contact and plastic deformation. A pre-oxidation treatment that yields such an oxide layer will lower overall wear and limit subsurface deformation compared to an as-deposited coating.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a conventional metal substrate (e.g., steel)
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment (800 °C in a low partial-pressure oxygen environment for 1 hour) to form a continuous oxide scale before sliding tests
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., around 400 °C under representative normal loads) that mimic service environments
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous and adherent oxide scale (potentially a spinel or mixed oxide) formed during the pre-oxidation process
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer limits direct metallic contact and local stress concentrations by distributing the load, thereby reducing both the wear rate (macroscopic wear) and the degree of plastic deformation (microscopic deformation). In the absence of this stable oxide, dynamic oxide formation during sliding leads to cracking and less effective protection, which increases wear and deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (as-deposited) coating, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced subsurface plastic deformation under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating without any pre-oxidation treatment
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under high-temperature conditions typical of the intended application. At lower temperatures or under extreme thermal cycling where the protective oxide may not form or may become unstable, the predicted benefits may not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, thickness and long-term stability of the oxide layer, as well as potential interactions with the substrate, remain uncertain. Further real-time characterization is required to fully elucidate the evolution of the oxide film during sliding.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on a steel substrate: one set as-deposited and one set pre-oxidized via heat treatment at 800 °C in low partial-pressure oxygen for 1 hour. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests (e.g., at 400 °C under the same normal load and sliding speed). Use in situ high-temperature microscopy and post-test cross-sectional analysis to observe the oxide layer integrity, wear track morphology, and subsurface deformation.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., volume loss per sliding distance)
Integrity and thickness of the oxide scale (via in situ/scanning techniques)
Subsurface microstructural changes (grain refinement, deformation features)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and subsurface deformation compared to the as-deposited coating, or if a stable, continuous oxide scale is not observed to persist during sliding, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi coating (PMC7512501) showed improved wear resistance over a lower-melting substrate, indicating that 3d-transition-element HEA coatings benefit from a multi-principal-element matrix and solid-solution strengthening. Later studies of CoCrFeMnNi under friction (PMC7311485) revealed an ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer that formed dynamically, reducing wear. More recently, FeCoNiMnCu (PMC10908794) demonstrated that high-temperature tribological performance can be tied to protective oxide spinels that form in situ. However, no prior report isolates how a FeNiCrCoCu coating specifically evolves under high-temperature sliding, leaving the precise mechanism governing wear and micro-deformation insufficiently understood.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether the dominant factor at elevated temperatures is strictly the dynamic tribofilm/oxide layer formation, or if near-surface microstructural evolution (grain refinement, dislocation substructure) more fundamentally governs wear resistance and local plasticity in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
decision.lever: Introduce a baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating on steel and compare it with an identical coating subjected to a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment (e.g., 800 °C in low partial-pressure oxygen for 1 hour), then measure wear and sub-surface microstructure evolution under high-temperature sliding. Track the tribofilm’s thickness and oxide chemistry via real-time high-temperature tribometry coupled with in-situ scanning techniques.
decision.why: If a pre-formed, stable oxide or nitride scale is indeed the key to limiting both macro-scale wear and micro-scale deformation, then pre-oxidation should lower wear rates and reduce sub-surface deformation relative to an as-deposited, untreated coating. Conversely, if wear and deformation do not improve with pre-oxidation, or if the protective film does not form in situ, the hypothesis of oxide-layer-controlled tribological behavior would be falsified.
